summary: Nicodemus, a leading Pharisee, comes to Jesus by night, and Jesus tells him he must be born again and that God gave His Son so believers may live.
key_insight: Nicodemus began, “we know.” Jesus answered, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and do not know these things?” The respected teacher came with credentials, and Jesus told him he needed a new birth from God.
story: Among the Pharisees was a man named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said, “Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher come from God; for no one can do these signs that You do unless God is with him.”

Jesus answered, “Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” Nicodemus asked, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”

Jesus answered, “Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. “The wind blows where it wishes,” He said; people hear its sound but cannot tell where it comes from or where it goes. “So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

“How can these things be?” Nicodemus asked. Jesus answered, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and do not know these things?” He spoke of what He knew and had seen. No one has ascended to heaven but the Son of Man, who came down from heaven.
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life.”

“For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life.” God sent His Son not to condemn the world but to save it, and whoever believes in Him is not condemned. The light has come into the world, but “men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.” Yet whoever does the truth comes to the light.

scene.label: Nicodemus
scene.text: He was a Pharisee and “a ruler of the Jews,” probably a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council in Jerusalem; John later says he was “one of them” (John 7:50). Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel,” a recognized teacher of the law. The signs he mentions were those Jesus did in Jerusalem at the Passover (John 2:23).

scene.label: By night
scene.text: John does not say why Nicodemus came at night. He may have feared being seen, or wanted an unhurried talk away from the crowds. In John’s Gospel, night and darkness often picture not yet seeing the truth (3:19; 13:30).

scene.label: “Born again”
scene.text: The Greek word can mean “again” or “from above.” Nicodemus heard “again” and pictured a second physical birth. Jesus’ words about the Spirit show that this birth is from above: God’s work, not man’s.

scene.label: Water and the Spirit
scene.text: Christians read this phrase in several ways. Many connect it to Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises to “sprinkle clean water on you” and put His Spirit within, one new birth that cleanses and gives life, something a teacher of Israel should have known. Others see water as natural birth, or as baptism. Views differ, but all agree the new birth is God’s work by His Spirit.

scene.label: The bronze serpent
scene.text: In Numbers 21:4–9, Israelites bitten by snakes in the wilderness were dying. God told Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived. In John, “lifted up” points to the cross (John 12:32–33).

witnesses.john: Only John records this conversation. It is the first of his long one-on-one talks: here Jesus speaks with a respected insider at night, and in the next chapter with a Samaritan woman at noon. John follows Nicodemus beyond this night, to his defense of Jesus before the council (7:50–51) and his costly gift of myrrh and aloes at Jesus’ burial (19:39).

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the One who came down from heaven and must be lifted up: the only Son whom God gave because He loved the world.
seeing.living: Nicodemus had learning, rank and respect, and none of it could give him new birth. Life in God’s kingdom begins as a gift of His Spirit, received by looking in faith to the Son lifted up, the way dying Israelites looked at the serpent. No one is too respectable to need it, or too far gone to receive it.
seeing.ponder: Are you still trying to come to God on the strength of what you know and have done, or have you looked to Jesus lifted up and received new life?

preaching.big_idea: Even the best teacher must be born again, and new birth comes by looking to the lifted-up Son.
outline: A respected man comes by night (1–2)
preaching.watch_for: The NKJV prints verses 16–21 as Jesus’ words; many scholars think John himself comments from verse 16 on, since the original had no quotation marks. Either way, verse 16 begins with “For” and explains why the Son must be lifted up.

title: Jesus and Nicodemus
